Alex — thanks for the clear constraints. High-level summary up front: PrivateLink (interface VPC endpoint) as the primary ingress gives the best security posture and least public attack surface for a provider-managed service; VPC Peering is lower-latency and cheaper for very high-bandwidth intra-VPC communication but doesn’t offer the same fine-grained service-level controls or cross-account access management; site-to-site VPN is appropriate for on-prem systems that need direct L3 reachability, and could be used as a DR/fallback path but is generally higher jitter/latency and operationally heavier to scale for bursty traffic.

Tradeoffs (short):
- Latency: Peering <= PrivateLink <= S2S VPN. Peering avoids ENI hop; PrivateLink adds an extra ENI/NLB hop which usually adds a few ms but is stable. VPN can be unpredictable based on transit.
- Security & access control: PrivateLink wins — service is reachable only via endpoint ENIs; you control which subnets/users can call it. Peering requires careful route table + NACL/SG rules and can be overly permissive if not tightly scoped. VPN exposes L3/GRE and is broader.
- Transitivity & cross-account: Peering is not transitive and doesn’t work across regions without extra setup; PrivateLink supports cross-account consumer endpoints cleanly and allows the provider to enforce ACLs.
- Throughput & scaling: Peering supports very high throughput; PrivateLink is backed by NLB & ENIs — throughput is fine for request/response workloads but you should size for concurrent connections and watch NLB connection limits; VPN throughput depends on the tunnel capacity and can be a bottleneck for spikes.
- Observability & troubleshooting: PrivateLink centralizes the service in Redwood’s account but you can provide VPC flow logs + ALB/NLB logs and per-endpoint metrics. Peering requires shared monitoring and agreed alerting.
- Cost: Peering has low per-GB cost inside the same region; PrivateLink has hourly endpoint + per-GB charges; VPN has appliance/tunnel costs and potential egress charges.

Recommendation (pilot):
1) Use PrivateLink as the production ingress for the pilot to satisfy "no internet exposure" and give Greenbank the ability to control which subnets/users can access the endpoint.
2) Maintain a short-lived VPC Peering connection (provider-to-management) for high-volume internal telemetry (metrics, snapshot upload) where latency and throughput matter and strict service-level isolation is less critical.
3) Offer an option to configure site-to-site VPN to on-prem for DR/backchannel and for specific on-prem hosts that must reach private resources at L3.

Operational asks from Greenbank for pilot:
- CIDR ranges to allow for endpoint ENIs + any peering (we do not accept overlapping CIDRs)
- IAM principal(s) that can accept VPC endpoint connections / sign endpoint policies
- KMS key ARN if you want us to integrate with customer-managed key flow for egress encryption
- TLS certs / hostname that you require on the NLB (we support TLS passthrough or termination at NLB)
- Contact info for your network/security reviewer

I’ll attach a short comparison matrix and a MAP (mutual action plan) with milestones. Will loop Kim and Marcus for the detailed technical checklist.

- Aditya

Quick technical notes from infra side:
- PrivateLink details: we expose the inference endpoint behind an NLB and publish it as a VPC Endpoint Service. Consumer creates interface endpoint(s) in their VPC which create ENIs in their subnets. Important operational items: ENI quota (per-AZ) on your side, endpoint acceptance policy (we can require manual acceptance or auto-accept for your account id), and security groups that only allow 443/TLS inbound from your subnets.
- TLS: we can terminate at NLB (recommended for observability) or do passthrough if you need end-to-end cert control. If you want us not to terminate, we’ll need the cert chain and coordination for SNI routing.
- Cross-AZ egress costs: PrivateLink consumes cross-AZ traffic; ensure you account for inter-AZ data transfer if your callers are in different AZs than our NLB-backed ENIs.
- Latency: for p99 <=50ms, PrivateLink will usually be fine if callers are in the same region and AZ — confirm AZ placement for consumers to avoid extra hops.
- Peering caveat: peering means the destination is routable at L3. This is handy for debug/backchannel but requires strict route table discipline to avoid exposing other services.

I’ll prepare a short operations checklist (quota checks, endpoint acceptance process, security group rules, flow logs) and paste it into the MAP.

— Kim
Kimberly Park

Operational engineering notes / risks to highlight:
- Concurrent connections & NLB: for bursty ~2k TPS spikes we need to ensure NLB connection capacity and tune the backend keepalive. Recommend running a small load test in staging to capture 95/99th connection counts and ensure target group scaling behavior.
- KV cache / large payloads: if Greenbank plans to stream large payloads (attachments, model snapshots), peering will be more efficient for bulk transfer; PrivateLink is optimized for API-style request/response.
- ENI quotas & IP exhaustion: consumer side must validate ENI per-subnet quotas. Provide target subnets (private subnets) where endpoints will be created.
- Metrics: we will publish per-endpoint metrics (accepted connections, TLS handshake errors) and can federate logs to a bucket in your account for audit if you want.
- VPN for DR: if you want S2S, suggest using a managed VPN (Transit Gateway + VPN or AWS Site-to-Site) with BGP. Configure Dead Peer Detection/BFD if supported for faster failover.

I can run the staging load test once we have an endpoint and test credentials.

— Marcus
